section_summary: This section contains Japanese regulatory procedures and commodity schedules for the reporting, confiscation, and reallocation of hoarded and excess materials to the Industrial Reconstruction Kodan. It also includes State Department correspondence discussing analytical research by the Division of Research for the Far East on Japanese economic self-support and regional trade. Finally, it features a comprehensive report by SCAP's Economic and Scientific Section evaluating Japan's 1947 economic conditions—focusing on industrial production, foreign trade deficits, severe inflation, and staple food supplies—along with forecasts for 1948.

subfiles.about: Japanese Cabinet instruction establishing procedures and commodity lists for the reporting, surrender, and transfer of hoarded, illegally held, and excess goods to the Industrial Reconstruction Kodan.
keywords: Temporary Demand and Supply Adjustment Law
subfiles.summary: This Japanese government instruction sets forth procedures for identifying, confiscating, and transferring illegally held, illegally acquired, and excess designated materials to the Industrial Reconstruction Kodan under the Temporary Demand and Supply Adjustment Law. It defines official valuation rules, appeal procedures through Regional Economic Stabilization Offices, and penalties for false reporting or failure to transfer, while exempting Allied military personnel and family household goods. Detailed attached schedules specify retention quotas and excess thresholds for fuels, metals, chemicals, textiles, and staple foodstuffs.
subfiles.title: Cabinet Instruction on Regulations for the Disposal and Transfer of Excess and Illegally Held Materials

subfiles.about: A comprehensive report reviewing Japan's 1947 industrial production, foreign trade, commodity prices, living costs, and wages, with projections for 1948.
subfiles.from: Research and Statistics Division, Economic and Scientific Section, GHQ SCAP
subfiles.summary: This report reviews Japan's economic performance in 1947, showing that industrial production recovered to 41 percent of the prewar average through indigenous coal and hydroelectric output but was constrained by raw material shortages. Persistent inflation was driven by food deficits, black-market transactions, and government budget deficits resulting from widespread failure to collect personal income taxes. Foreign trade registered a 335 million dollar deficit covered largely by United States aid for food imports, while export expansion was hampered by cotton import delays and a severe shortage of dollar exchange. The report forecasts a potential 25 to 30 percent increase in industrial activity for 1948 contingent on foreign raw material financing, improved coal distribution, and effective tax and price stabilization.
subfiles.title: Economic Conditions in Japan
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
